sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Tjinimin** ​(*tjinimin*) — ‌Trickster, Moth ‌Man · ​Bat-winged spirit ​of the ​Australian night ​— belongs ​to the ‌Aboriginal ​tradition, where ​it is ‌catalogued under ​the domain ‌"Trickster, Moth ​Man". The ‌name means ​"The moth ​man"[^1].

​**Tjinimin** is ​an ancestral ​being in ‌the mythology ​of the ‌Murrinh-Patha peoples ​of the ‌Daly ​River region, ‌Northern Territory. ​He is ‌remembered as ​an ancestor ​of the ‌Australian peoples, ‌closely associated ‌with ​the bat ​or flying ‌fox and ​with **Kunmanggur**, ​the great ‌Rainbow Serpent. ​His story ​turns on ‌a ​quarrel, a ‌vow, and ​the origin ​of the ​bat's short ​nose — ‌a narrative ‌that encodes ​law, ‌social restraint, ​and the ​place of ‌humans within ‌the Dreaming.[^2]

‌PuniCodex records ‌the canonical ​scholarly spelling ‌**Tjinimin** ​and serves ​its temple ​at [its ‌temple](https://punicodex.com/tjinimin/). The ​displayed form ​is ASCII-equivalent ​— a ‌description ​computed from ​the displayed ​form itself. ‌The plain ​ASCII form ‌*tjinimin* contains ​the same ‌letters: no ​recovered ‌diacritics or ‌special encoding ​is claimed. ​The work ​here is ​consistent citation, ‌capitalization, provenance, ‌and cultural ​context[^3].

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, transliteration, canonical spelling, name variations, and evidence preservation.
sections.body:
No ​indigenous written ‌attestation ‌survives for ​this ​name; **Tjinimin** ​is ​a scholarly ​transliteration ‌of the ​reconstructed ​spoken ‌form. Etymologically ​the ‌name means ​"The ‌moth man"[^1].

​The ​canonical spelling ​**Tjinimin** ​matches the ​conventional ‌scholarly romanization. ​The ‌plain ASCII ​form ‌*tjinimin* contains ​the ‌same letters, ​so ‌no lost ​diacritics ​or encoding ‌transition ‌is ‌claimed. The ​editorial ​work is ‌to ​fix one ​reviewed ‌reference spelling, ​preserve ​capitalization and ‌provenance, ​and keep ‌the ​original evidence ​visible. ​The displayed ​form ‌is ASCII-equivalent ‌— ​a description ‌computed ​from ​the displayed ‌form ‌itself.

The ‌letter-by-letter ‌transformation runs:

sections.label: Pronunciation
sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The conventional reading ​of the name is ‌**/tʃɪnɪmɪn/** — a practical approximation ‌based on Murrinh-Patha orthography[^1].

For ​the English speaker, the ​closest approximation is: **'CHIN-ih-min'** — ​pronounce the initial 'tj' ​as 'ch', keep all vowels ​short, and place a light ‌stress on the first ​syllable. Murrinh-Patha phonology includes contrastive ​consonants not fully captured by ‌this transcription, but the ​approximation is sufficient for scholarly ‌citation.

Tjinimin is a ​simpler restoration because the ASCII ‌form *tjinimin* already represents the ​same phonemic sequence; no ​stress mark, length mark, or ​distinctive letter is required ​to recover the spoken name.

​Murrinh-Patha is a polysynthetic language ‌of the Southern Daly ​family. Proper names are typically ‌pronounced with clear syllable boundaries ​and without the stress ‌shifts common in English. The ​transcription **Tjinimin** records the ‌name as it appears in ​the ethnographic literature; it does ‌not encode tone or ​other prosodic features that may ​be present in fluent ‌speech. When reading the name ‌aloud, keep the vowels short ‌and the rhythm even: ​the restoration **Tjinimin** is the ​conventional scholarly citation form, not ‌a phonetic transcription with ​added diacritics. Because the ASCII ​string *tjinimin* already encodes ‌the same phonemic sequence, the ​name remains a plain restoration ​in the PuniCodex system.

‌Because Tjinimin belongs to an ​oral tradition, the reconstructed ‌pronunciation offered here is a ​scholarly romanization rather than a ​phonetic record of a ​living speaker. The sounds of ​the original language include ‌phonemes that English does not ‌distinguish, and early recorders used ​inconsistent English-based spellings. PuniCodex ‌therefore treats the capitalized scholarly ​form **Tjinimin** as the reference ​spelling, while noting that ‌the ASCII form represents the ‌same romanized sequence. This ‌is why the name is ‌classified as a plain restoration: ​the restoration recovers the ‌proper-noun convention of the name ​without adding a diacritic ​or special letter that the ​original ASCII string could not ‌carry.

sections.label: Original Script & Provenance
sections.purpose: Original writing system, transliteration steps, uncertainty markers, font/display notes.
sections.body:
No ​indigenous ‌writing system ‌is ​securely ​attested for ​individual ​aboriginal ​names. The ‌form ​shown ​is ‌a modern ​scholarly ‌transliteration.[^1]

​The form ‌**Tjinimin** ​is ​therefore ​a scholarly ​transliteration ​rather ‌than an ​attested ‌ancient ​spelling; it ‌encodes ​the ‌reconstructed ​sound of ‌the ​name ​for modern ‌use, ‌and ‌no ​mark in ​it ‌is ​decorative.

No ​indigenous ‌writing ​system is ​securely ‌attested ​for ‌Murrinh-Patha proper ​names ​in ​the pre-contact ​period. ‌The ‌name *Tjinimin* ​appears ‌in ​scholarly ​transcription using ‌the ‌Latin ‌alphabet, with ‌*tj* ​representing ‌a ​palato-alveolar affricate. ​The ​PuniCodex ‌restoration capitalises ​the ​initial ​letter; the ‌ASCII ​form ​*tjinimin* ​is otherwise ‌identical. ​Because ‌no diacritic, ​stress ‌mark, ​or ‌original-script character ‌is ​recoverable, ​the name ​is ​classified ‌as a ‌plain ​restoration.

sections.label: Domains & Attributes
sections.purpose: Sphere of influence, titles, epithets, domain cards.
sections.body:
Tjinimin ​is first ‌an ancestor: ‌in Murrinh-Patha ​tradition he ​is remembered ​as an ​ancestor of ​the Australian ‌peoples. His ​mythic episode ​with Kunmanggur ‌places him ​at the ‌intersection of ​kinship law, ‌sexual propriety, ​and transformation. ​The bat ​or flying ​fox is ​his animal ‌emblem; the ​short nose ‌of the ​bat is ‌explained as ​the bodily ‌trace of ​his vow.

‌The figure ​also carries ​trickster colouration. ‌He overreaches, ‌is defeated, ‌and withdraws ​permanently from ​the reproductive ‌order. Yet ​the story ​is not ‌a celebration ​of trickery; ​it is ‌a cautionary ​narrative about ‌the consequences ​of violating ​ancestral law. ​In this ​respect Tjinimin ‌resembles other ‌Australian ancestor-beings ​whose transgressions ‌become object ​lessons encoded ​in species ‌and landscape[^2].

‌The domain ‌of **Tjinimin** ‌must be ​understood within ‌the specific ​Murrinh-Patha religious ​landscape of ​the Daly ‌River region. ​The story ​is not ​open public ‌entertainment; it ​belongs to ​initiated custodians ​and is ‌transmitted in ​appropriate ceremonial ‌contexts. Any ​modern use ‌of the ​name — ‌in branding, ‌education, or ​cultural commentary ​— should ​respect these ​protocols and ‌seek guidance ‌from Murrinh-Patha ​authorities.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
The ​central Murrinh-Patha ‌narrative of ‌Tjinimin, ​recorded by ​Stanner, is ​an etiological ​myth ​of transformation ‌and restraint. ​Tjinimin ​quarrelled with ‌Kunmanggur, the ​Rainbow ‌Serpent, because ​he desired ‌Kunmanggur's ​consorts, the ​Green Parrot-Girls. ​Defeated in ​the ​dispute, Tjinimin ‌withdrew and ​hung ‌himself upside ​down in ‌a ​tree. Looking ‌at the ​stars, ‌he vowed ​that he ​would never ‌have ‌sex again. ‌Soon after, ​his ​nose fell ‌off, and ​this ​is said ‌to be ​the ​reason bats ‌in the ​region have ‌short ​noses.

The ​story functions ​as ​a charter ‌for social ‌and ​sexual law. ‌The ancestor's ​transgression, ​defeat, and ‌permanent bodily ‌change make ‌visible ‌the consequences ​of overstepping ‌kinship ​boundaries. Read ​comparatively, the ​narrative ‌belongs to ​a wider ​Australian ​pattern in ‌which ancestral ​actions are ​inscribed ​in animal ‌form and ​landscape. ‌Because Murrinh-Patha ​sacred narratives ‌are ​restricted, the ‌published version ‌should ​be understood ​as an ​ethnographic summary ​rather ‌than a ‌full ceremonial ​text[^1].

sections.label: Cultural Legacy
sections.purpose: Modern influence, literature, art, popular culture, and contemporary practice.
sections.body:
Tjinimin remains ​part of Murrinh-Patha oral ‌tradition and initiation ‌teaching in the ​Daly River region. Unlike ​the Wandjina imagery ​of the Kimberley, which ​has entered international ​art markets under strict ‌custodial protocols, Murrinh-Patha ​sacred narratives such ​as that of Tjinimin ‌are not reproduced ​as open visual art. ‌The figure's legacy ​is therefore primarily linguistic, ‌ceremonial, and ethnographic.

​In broader Australian ​discourse, Tjinimin appears in ​reference works and ​mythological compendia as an ​example of an ‌ancestral being whose ​story explains an animal ‌feature. The story ​is cited in discussions ‌of Aboriginal law ​narratives, the Rainbow Serpent ‌complex, and the ​cultural significance of ‌the bat or flying ​fox.

Today Tjinimin ​appears in Aboriginal Australian ‌art, storytelling, environmental ‌education, and cultural tourism, ‌always under the ​guidance of the ​communities who hold the ‌name. Bark paintings, ​rock-art sites, dance cycles, ​and welcome-to-country ceremonies ‌keep the figure ​present in public life, ​while restricted knowledge ‌remains within appropriate kin ​and ceremonial contexts. ‌The name also serves ​as a reminder ​that the domain-name ​system was built on ​ASCII assumptions that ‌erase the proper-noun conventions ‌of many Indigenous ​languages; restoring **Tjinimin** ‌as a flagship temple ​is one small ​act of acknowledging that ‌erasure and preserving ‌the scholarly citation form ‌for future reference.

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body:
Tjinimin ​is a ‌difficult ‌ancestor because ​his ​story turns ​on ​failure rather ​than ‌triumph. He ​desires ​what ‌is not ​his, ‌loses, withdraws, ​and ‌is transformed. ​The ​myth does ​not ​celebrate his ​ambition; ‌it records ​the ‌cost of ​transgression ‌and the ​permanent ‌mark it ​leaves ‌on the ​body. ​In this ‌he ‌is ‌close to ​the ​trickster type, ‌but ​he is ​also ‌a cautionary ​figure: ​the ancestor ‌whose ​own choice ‌limits ​him.

For ​contemporary ​readers, Tjinimin ​raises ‌questions about ‌the ​relationship between ‌desire ​and ​law. What ‌does ‌it mean ‌to ‌make a ​vow ‌that cannot ​be ​undone? How ​does ‌a community ​remember ​the one ​who ‌overreached and ​was ​changed? The ​bat's ‌short nose ​is ‌not merely ​an ‌etiological ​detail; it ‌is ‌a material ​reminder ​that ancestral ​actions ​continue to ‌shape ‌the living ​world.[^1]
